title: Sunita the flower-scavenger
hookLine: a man of the lowest caste, sweeping discarded flowers, is invited to ordain (Theragatha, Sunita)

cards: Born in a low family. Poor. Little to eat.
That's how Sunita describes himself in his verses in the Theragatha, the poems of the elder monks. His work was lowly too, he says: he carried away withered flowers, the ones people had thrown out.
People despised him and looked down on him, and he kept his mind humble and bowed to many. Then one day he saw the Buddha walking into the chief city of Magadha, with the company of monks around him.
Today, what happened on that street.

teach.b: First, the pole. Sunita sets down his carrying pole and goes to pay his respects. And in his verse, the Buddha, the highest of men, stops and stands still, out of compassion for him.
Sunita bows at the Teacher's feet, stands to one side, and asks to go forth, to become a monk. Third, the answer.

The Buddha, compassionate toward the whole world, says, come, monk. And Sunita says: that was my ordination. Two words, spoken on a street, to a man whose job was clearing away other people's dead flowers.
Fourth, the end of the poem. He goes off alone into the forest and practices as the Teacher taught him, and the verses say he reached the end of the path.

Then the gods come and honor him with joined palms, and the Buddha smiles and speaks a verse: by austerity, by the holy life, by restraint and taming, this is how one becomes a brahmin; this is the highest brahminhood.
The word brahmin is still there, but in the Buddha's mouth it's about how someone lives, not the family they were born to. The man people stepped around becomes the one the gods bow to.
And the first thing that happened to him wasn't a test. It was a welcome.

how: Teachers retell Sunita's story when speaking of the Buddha's welcome to people of every background, and Sunita's verses are read as part of the Theragatha, the collection of poems by the early elder monks.

o: a brahmin who taught at the court
a prince who gave up his kingdom
a flower-scavenger welcomed as a monk

p: a brahmin by how one lives

s: Sunita had to wait a long time before he was allowed to ordain
the Buddha said, come, monk, right there, and that was his ordination.
Sunita describes himself as poor and looked down on
his verses say he was born in a low family, with little to eat, and despised.
the Buddha walked past without stopping
in Sunita's verse he stood still out of compassion.

games.q: you're Sunita, carrying your pole of withered flowers, and the Buddha comes walking up the street with his monks. what do you do?
o: step aside and keep your head down.
set down your pole and go to pay respects.
hurry off before anyone sees you.
games.why: he sets down the pole and bows, the Buddha stands still for him, and when Sunita asks to go forth, the answer is: come, monk.

practice: Picture the people your days pass by without a word: whoever empties the bins at work, cleans the restroom, drops off the delivery.
Choose one face, or one role, and hold them in mind for a few breaths, the way the Buddha stopped on the street. Let a plain wish for their well-being come.

wordCard.voice: Sunita. The poor flower-scavenger, despised for his low birth, whom the Buddha stopped for and welcomed with two words: come, monk.

orig.note: Pali: come, monk; Sunita says those words were his ordination.

carryVoice: Your line: the sweeper was welcome. Honor, in that verse, comes from how a person lives. That's day seven hundred seventy-three.
